utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The siege of Sarajevo, as it came to be popularly known, was an episode of such notoriety in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia that one must go back to World War II to find a parallel in European history. Not since then had a professional army conducted a campaign of unrelenting violence against the inhabitants of a European city so as to reduce them to a state of medieval deprivation in which they were in constant fear of death. In the period covered in this indictment, there was nowhere safe for a Sarajevan, not at home, at school, in a hospital, from deliberate attack. Why did it happen? Sarajevo, a city of half a million people, was the capital of the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a federal unit of the former Yugoslavia. Its main ethnic composition was approximately 44 per cent Bosniak, and by that term I mean Bosnians of the Muslim community; 31 per cent Serb, and 17 per cent Croat. In 1991, first Slovenia, then Croatia, declared independence and subsided into violent ethnic conflict. As Yugoslavia disintegrated the government determined to follow the lead of Slovenia and Croatia in declaring independence and in March 1992 declared itself to be the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sarajevo was a thriving multi-ethnic community, proud of a rich cultural heritage and its international status as the 1984 Winter Olympic city. Many remained convinced that their city was too urban, sophisticated and contentedly multi-ethnic to suffer such a fate. The end of peace came in early April 1992. Sarajevans had observed forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, or JNA, conducting exercises around Sarajevo, and when on 6 April the European community recognised the Republic, hostilities began. The following day Bosnian Serbs declared themselves to be the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, better known from August 1992 as the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and claimed the majority of the territory of the Republic. I will hereafter refer to it as the Republika Srpska. The objective of the Republika Srpska in relation to Sarajevo was clear by May 1992. On the 12th of May, its National Assembly stated their strategic objective to be the "partition of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts." The same day, the assembly voted to create the Army of the Republika Srpska, or Vojska Republika Srpska, known as the VRS, effectively transforming remaining JNA units and other forces loyal to the Republika Srpska into commands of the new VRS. The particular VRS corps which was deployed in the Sarajevan theatre was the Sarajevsko Romanijski Korpus or Sarajevo Romanija Corps, known as the SRK. The army of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the Armija Bosna i Herzegovina, known as the ABiH. So the two principle protagonists were the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the break-away Republika Srpska, operating through their respective armies; the ABiH and the SRK. Over the next three and a half years, the people of Sarajevo descended into what some observers described at the time as a medieval hell. The two armies fought to a position of stalemate, the confrontation lines became static, and reflecting the protracted strangle hold of the SRK, the battle became known as the siege of Sarajevo. The stand-off came about because, although the ABiH had approximately 75.000 soldiers committed to the battle and the SRK only about 18.000, the SRK had a countervailing territorial and armament advantage. It held the high ground encircling the city and had far more artillery. By January 1993, Sarajevo was surrounded by hundreds of pieces of artillery, including tanks, howitzers, anti-aircraft guns and other weapons. Neither side could deliver the decisive blow. Nevertheless, the SRK could keep engaged in Sarajevo and therefore, out of the rest of the Bosnian theatre, three or four ABiH troops for every one of theirs. Further, by moderating the intensity of both legitimate and unlawful attacks on Sarajevo, Republika Srpska could exert pressure on its opponent at critical times. For long periods, the residents of this European city were deprived of water, gas, and electricity. Without these essential services, they were regularly forced from the relative safety of their homes in order to queue at water pumps and scrounge firewood, which they would burn in ingeniously instructed stoves for cooking and warmth. For those in high-rise buildings, periods of no electricity meant no elevators in which to carry up their water, fuel, and other essentials. But there was another, darker, dimension to this armed conflict. It soon became apparent that civilians who chose to remain within Sarajevo, within the confrontation lines, were being deliberately targeted. Through television and the print media, the world watched in horror as the people of Sarajevo were fired upon at will as they crossed lines of sight from the SRK-held hills and high-rise buildings. Occupation, age, sex, and ethnic background were irrelevant to the sniper. The indictment has annexed to it some illustrations. A three-year-old child was shot at the door of her home, a nine-year-old as she played in her garden. Civilians were shot in their homes as they watched television, drank coffee, or prayed. They were shot outside their homes as they crossed the street, collected wood, drew water from canals, carried it home, cleared rubbish, chatted and walked with friends, rode in cars, trucks, buses, and trams, on bicycles and buried their dead. It seems no area of human activity was too innocuous, mundane, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or sacrosanct to escape the sniper's judgement. Serbs who chose to stay were unforgiven and shot along with their Muslim fellow Sarajevans. In order to maintain a semblance of order and thwart attacks, the dead were buried at night, or during fogs, or simply in odd plots of earth between buildings. New tracks and back routes protected by buildings from known sniper position were used instead of exposed foot paths and roads. Anti-sniping barriers were erected to the same end. Shipping containers, buses, trucks, and other obstacles were placed across intersections which were vulnerable to the SRK positions. The snipers responded to this new challenge by making the most of gaps between the barricades, anticipating when victims would be fleetingly vulnerable. Nowhere, however, was safe from the shelling. The Prosecution will call expert evidence to explain that the artillery which the SRK deployed included both direct fire and indirect-fire weaponry. Direct fire weapons, such as tanks, howitzers, and large calibre guns, as, for instance, anti-aircraft guns and armoured personnel carrier guns, APCs, usually fire along a direct line of sight. Mortars, on the other hand, are designed to travel on an inverted U-shaped trajectory so that they fall into areas which cannot be seen by the mortar crew. Accordingly, they are operated by a crew in radio communication with a forward observer who directs their fire to the target. A mortar shell is specifically designed to kill and maim people. It is not usually used to destroy property. Its casing becomes shrapnel designed to inflict the maximum number of casualties. What's left at the point of impact, if it's a hard surface such as a road, is usually a small indentation. By the end of the war, the streets, foot paths, and parking lots of Sarajevo were peppered with the telltale star pattern of mortar impacts known as mortar roses. During the period covered by the indictment, mortars were used by the SRK to a devastating effect against civilians engaged in a variety of activities where they congregated in the open out of a direct line of sight with SRK positions. For instance, a soccer game, waterline cues, groups of playing children, a crowded secluded marketplace, schools, hospitals and even funeral processions. The scheduled shelling incidents demonstrates some of these. This campaign of deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians is the foundation of the Prosecution case against Major General Galic. It is important to note at this point that the Prosecution case, as set out in its pre-trial brief, is that shelling was used sometimes with the intention of hitting a specific target of civilians and at other times indiscriminately against civilians. That is, the crew would deliberately fire shells into known civilian areas not necessarily with the intention of hitting a particular target of civilians but rather with the knowledge that wherever it landed, it was likely to endanger civilians. To place it in its proper legal context, this practice offended the principle of distinction, to which I will later refer. The world watched in disbelief that the perpetrators acted with impunity, day after day, week after week, month after month, year after year. It so tore at the world's conscience that, in no small measure, it contributed to the establishment of this Tribunal. During the three and a half years of the battle of Sarajevo, there were three principle commanders of the SRK. The second of those three, Major General Stanislav Galic, who I will hereafter usually refer to as the accused, was the commander for the longest period, almost two years, from around the 10th of September, 1992 to the 10th of August, 1994. So far I have frequently referred to the battle in terms which cover its entirety rather than specifically to the indictment period, which corresponds to the accused's tenure as commander of the SRK. Indeed, the Chamber will shortly view a collage of video clips which predate the indictment period, as well as portray events during it. The reasons are three-fold. Firstly, it is the Prosecution case that the accused inherited a pre-existing strategy of the deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians. Secondly, the characteristics of the campaign, before, during, and even after his tenure, are essentially identical. Thirdly, I mean to place the accused's actions in their proper historical context. Naturally, the accused is only accountable for the responsibilities which fell to him as a result of his period as commander. Even in relation to the indictment period, the Prosecution does not say that all wrongdoing was attributable to the accused or indeed that all wrongdoing was perpetrated from the accused's side of the confrontation lines. There is evidence that civilians on both sides of the confrontation lines were deliberately targeted. It is trite to observe that unlawful behaviour against civilians by the accused's opponents did not entitle him to do likewise. I will now seek to acquaint the Chamber with the layout of Sarajevo. In so doing, I take the Trial Chamber to a diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, the map to which I now point depicts the city of Sarajevo. You will observe that there are two green lines, one lighter and one darker, which with encircle the city. The city appears as a developed area on the map. The two green lines depict the confrontation lines between the SRK and the ABiH. As I've already observed, those lines remained relatively static throughout the war. You will note that at some points, those lines came very close together, sometimes as close as 50 metres. At other points they were much further apart. I also point out that the lines at some points travelled into the urban area of the city. That applies to this area, which is the Grbavica area, and also to the left on the map in the area of Dobrinja. Dobrinja was the Olympic village for the 1984 Winter Olympics, and following that event it became a residential apartment block area. It adjoins the airport. The map also depicts the various scheduled sniping incidents, that is, where they took place, or more particularly, where the victims were at the time that they were shot. Those positions are depicted by the red dots. Your Honours will note that there is a reference to 27, but number 1 was a "U" beside it, and that is because, Mr. President, your predecessor descheduled that incident but allowed the Prosecution to continue to call evidence on it. So its current status is as an unscheduled sniping incident. The blue dots depict the places where the scheduled shelling incidents occurred. The reference to A, B, C, and so on are references to particular shells. So, for instance, shelling incident 1, which occurred in Dobrinja, involved two mortar shells, so in close proximity. Scheduled incident 4, which also occurred in Dobrinja, involved three shells. I also point out on the map a star, which marks the position of the Lukavica barracks. Those military barracks became the forward command post for the accused, and indeed they were his forward command post throughout the indictment period. The Trial Chamber will note the proximity of the barracks to the Dobrinja residential area. Your Honours, I appreciate that it is difficult from a map when one is not familiar with what it depicts to gain much from it. At this stage I simply make the point that the development of Sarajevo can be seen to run in an east/west line and to be relatively narrow. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I now take Your Honours to some photographs, and before I do that, I will lay a plastic sheet over the map to demonstrate where the photographs I'm about to take you to were taken from. The first photograph was taken from this position, Trebevic, and the two lines indicate what will be shortly seen in the photograph. So firstly, Your Honours will note that the camera was pointing approximately north, that is, from the southern edge of the city, looking across it, in a northwards direction, but within the photograph you will be able to see much of what lay to the west. I now take the Trial Chamber to that photograph. This is that photograph, and I'll wait until the video camera depicts it. Perhaps if the camera could zoom back to allow as much of the photograph to be seen at the same time. At this stage I'm concerned only with the top photograph. So this is a photograph taken from Trebevic looking across the city, encompassing more or less the developed area furthest to the east, and to the west we can see disappearing down the valley floor the rest of the city. I point out firstly some obvious geographical features. One can observe from this photograph that the city lies at the base of a valley floor, and indeed a river runs along it. One can also observe that towards the west, the valley floor -- indeed, the valley flattens out to a plain. If you come back to the eastern side of the city, the side to the east is sometimes called the old city, and in terms of the three principal communities of Sarajevo, it is a section associated with the Bosniak community, and indeed it is the oldest part of the city. There is an area towards the centre of the photograph which is known to be a focal point for the Croat Sarajevan community, or was before the war, at least. To the east, one notices that there are more high-rise modern buildings, and they were characterised by a more mixed community, and as such in the more modern area there was a large Bosnian Serb component amongst the residents. I now point out in the photograph the two principle hospitals of Sarajevo which were operating at the time. I should say that this photograph was taken last year, in the year 2000, but for my purposes, nothing much has changed since the indictment period. I firstly point out the grounds of the Kosevo hospital, which was a little up from the valley floor, towards the north of the city, and that was a large hospital complex. I now point out the second biggest hospital, which was known as the State Hospital, sometimes as the French Hospital. In the video collage which the Trial Chamber will later view, you will see a portion which shows a sniper's nest which was positioned coincidentally from around the same area as where this photograph was taken from. And this portion of this photograph can be seen through the hole from the sniper's nest which gave a view of the city, including the State Hospital and the site of one of these scheduled sniping incidents. I now point out the Marsal Tito barracks, will featured prominently in the pre-indictment period, and Your Honours will likely to hear evidence about it only in that context. Along the valley floor ran arterial roads, one in particular, which was the -- and remains the main communication link for vehicular traffic through the city of Sarajevo. That road travels more or less through the centre of the valley at this modern western end, and then, as it comes to the central part of the photograph, runs alongside the river, which is where I'm pointing at the moment. This photograph also shows the assembly building, another structure which featured prominently in the pre-indictment period, and as this photograph shows, at the time it was taken, still shows the signs of heavy shelling. The area of Grbavica is in the foreground beneath the ridge, which is immediately visible in the photograph. Your Honours, will hear much of Grbavica during the trial. It was the source of much sniping activity into the city and an area held by the SRK. I also point out, and it may be difficult for the video camera to pick it up - if the video camera could perhaps zoom in - the approximate position in the old city of the Markale market. That was a scene of the worst civilian devastation by shelling in one particular incident which occurred on the 5th of February, 1994, when one mortar shell, size 120 millimetre, killed 66 people who were attending the market at the time. The approximate direction of fire of that shell was from the Markovici area, which is behind a ridge, which probably cannot be easily made out by the video camera at about this point. In front of it, and to the left, is a well-known local position known as sharp stone, translation of sharp stone. That was a ridge which approximated the position of the confrontation lines at that point, so that the SRK occupied the plateau-like high ground and then beneath the ridge, a short distance away, was the confrontation line separating it from the ABiH. A number of sniping incidents occurred in that area beneath sharp stone, sharp stone being the source of fire. Your Honours, I return to the diagram with the plastic overlay, and I now point out the position of a second panorama photograph that I'll take you to. The lines indicate the position of the camera at the time this photograph was taken, which was just a few months ago, September/October 2001. The view which appears in the photograph encompasses Lukavica barracks and the area where number 3 scheduled shelling incidents occurred, as well as three scheduled sniping incidents. So the direction of the camera is approximately south/south-west. I come now to that photograph, and perhaps the camera in the first instance could zoom back as far as possible to give the viewers a sense of what is depicted overall. And I notice, Your Honours, that part of the photograph is obstructed by -- that's better. All right. Now, again it's apparent that this photograph was taken from high ground. You can see beneath the hill the apartment development of Dobrinja, which I said earlier was the village for the Winter Olympics of 1984, and in the foreground, the runway, or one of the runways, for the airport. Coming to the left of the photograph, you can see the words "Lukavica barracks," and I now point to that complex, which can be seen to be behind what appears in the photograph to be a white road at a T-intersection. On that T-intersection in particular, if you could zoom in - I'd be grateful if the camera could zoom in to this point where the pointer is - there appears to be a two-storey white building. That was of the office of the accused in his forward barracks. In particular, he was on the top floor, and in the front corner of the building, to the right. Moving further along the photograph, one comes to a church, and further again, one comes to the site of shelling incident 1 and sniping incident 6. I come back to the left of the photograph, and I'll shortly show you a diagram which will show the precise position of the confrontation lines, which was approximately at this point. Shelling incident 1 occurred in the forecourt of a U-shaped complex -- apartment complex. Virtually identical to the complex which can be seen immediately to its left. That is, three sides facing towards the hill where the camera is positioned. So that is virtually replicated behind the trees to the right. On that occasion, a soccer game was being held in a car park, to the right, and the direction of the two mortar shells was from the area of Lukavica. As I've earlier indicated, we can see in this photograph the approximate position of sniping incident 6. Your Honours, the nature of the individual crimes which constitute the crime base for the indictment are such that they are difficult to convey in a courtroom. In the case of sniping, they involve persons being shot in the open. In circumstances where the killer is secluded in the case of shelling, the use of indirect fire means that those who were present at the place where the shell landed generally did not see where the shell emanated from. The Prosecution is aware of the difficulties that these factors present to the Trial Chamber in understanding the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence which the Prosecution shall call. Traditional means of conveying a crime scene involve the use of photographs and maps, and indeed they would go part of the way to placing Your Honours in the position where the crime scene can be imagined, according to the evidence. In order to better assist the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution has prepared a video of each of the sniping and shelling incidents. In relation to the sniping incidents, if the victim survived and is available to give evidence, the victim was videoed at the scene, pointing out precisely where they were at the time they were hit. This exercise was undertaken in the last few months. If, however, the victim was fatally wounded, an eyewitness to the incident appears on the video, pointing out, to the best of their recollection, where the victim was at precisely the moment that they were shot. A member of the OTP is then seen to place a yellow cross on that precise spot according to the direction of the eyewitness or the surviving victim. Later, a tripod was erected over those yellow spots and the camera lens fixed at a height approximating the height of the point of entry on the body of the victim of the bullet. A professional photographer then took photographs depicting a 360-degree view from that position, the position where the bullet entered the body of the victim. These photographs were later joined up, with appropriate software, so that a continuous, 360-degree image can be made available to the Trial Chamber. It can be played in court, and by the use of the computer mouse, one can navigate in any direction, up and down, zooming in, and zooming out, panning back. Defence counsel, Ms. Pilipovic, was able to attend the filming of some of these incidents in September of this year. The scheduled shelling incidents were videoed in the same fashion. All of those who participated in the shooting of the video footage will be made available by the Prosecution to give evidence and to attest to the truth of what they are heard to say on the video and what they did on the video. In due course, and in that fashion, all of the video of the incidents will be tendered by the Prosecution. It will be tendered in edited form, but I hasten to add that an un-cut version has been disclosed to the Defence. The edited form will include a note at the commencement of each segment indicating the date on which it was filmed, the particular scheduled incident to which it relates, the names of all those who were present during the filming and their roles, for instance, investigator, interpreter, name of the witness, camera people, the GPS position of the site, that is, the global satellite positioning system, so that we are with best able to provide an accurate record of where that place was, and in the un-cut footage the GPS machine is held up to the camera lens so that the reading can be recorded. The direction of the video camera or in some cases video cameras were facing. When the panoramic photographs were taken, the camera invariably started off pointing north and then took a series of photographs around, so that it's possible to figure out what direction one is looking in as one and a navigates around the photographs. I will take you now to a sample incident using this technology, and the incident is sniping incident 6. The schedule for that incident reads: 11 July 1993, Munira Zametica a woman aged 48 years was shot dead while collecting water from the Dobrinja River in the area of Dobrinja 2 and 3. The scene of the killing therefore was the Dobrinja River, which flowed through Dobrinja in a cement-lined canal. Local residents would draw water from it, since the water supply to their homes had been cut off. The canal ran an approximately east/west direction from the direction of Lukavica. At this point I will show the Trial Chamber a diagram -- or should I say a portion of a larger map which has been blown up to illustrate the relevant details. Your Honours, perhaps I could have some assistance in having the -- that second map mounted higher than it presently is. This is a detail of the first map. It's electronically based so it's possible to blow up any particular portion of it. We see at the red dot the position of sniping incident 6, and the Trial Chamber -- I invite the Trial Chamber to note that nearby the two other sniping incidents, being 18 and 22. One can also see on this map the position of shelling incident 1, which is in this area that I indicate now. The large red circle is the position of the church which appeared on the panorama photograph. To the left of it can be seen the confrontation lines, light green being the most forward position of the ABiH forces, dark green being the most forward position of the SRK forces. The significance of the Mahine [phoen] church is that the Prosecution will call evidence that there was a regular pattern of sniping into the Dobrinja area from that building during the indictment period. As well, there was regular sniping from a part of a block of apartments which is marked by the small red dot. Indeed, it was a particular part of the apartment block that was occupied by the SRK. The evidence will indicate that the distance between the church and sniping incident 6 was around 900 metres, and between the apartment block and incident 6 was around 740 metres. The blue line is the Dobrinja River, although its appearance is more in the form of the concrete-lined canal. The witnesses will give evidence that typically, sniper fire came down the canal and alongside the canal. At various positions alongside it, since it traversed a heavily occupied residential area, were a collection of foot bridges, such as one immediately alongside incident 6, and wider road bridges, such as near incident 18. Barricades were erected on the bridges at different times. I point to another bridge behind incident 6. Those who collected water from --

utterances.text: -- were regularly subjected to fire and many others had been shot previously at around the same place as sniping incident 6. Sometimes the sniping would continue all day and day after day. This incident occurred beneath the foot bridge which I've earlier indicated. On the 11th of July, 1993, a sunny day, at about 2.00 p.m., the victim and a neighbour, [redacted], approached the bridge in order to draw water from the canal. They saw several people sheltering against the side of the concrete foundations of the bridge, which afforded them protection from the direction of the SRK positions. The people who were already there told them they had seen bullets hitting the water. The group then took turns to quickly venture from their protected position down to the water's edge to quickly fill their containers. One went, then another, and then the victim approached to fill her bucket. As she did so, she was hit in the chest. She turned and was hit by a bullet in the neck and fell. Her 16-year-old daughter was nearby and was summoned by those present. She came and saw her mother lying face down near the water's edge. She and the others were prevented from pulling the victim back to safety by continued gunfire. Her daughter saw the bullets hitting the water. The victim's son arrived and attempts were made to reach her, but they were always forced back by the continuing gunfire, until another neighbour obtained some rope and tied it around the arm of the victim, which enabled them all to then pull her to a more protected area, by which time she was dead. In the video, which Your Honours are about to view, the victim is a neighbour, (redacted), who accompanied her to the site and was standing alongside the concrete foundations a few metres from the victim at the time she was shot, was asked to indicate where firstly she was located at the time of the shooting and then where the victim was located at the precise moment she was shot. utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, do we have that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I have that photograph at the bar table in hard copy form, and I understand Your Honours have a copy of it. And I think my friends have a copy. I understand that they were given a copy, or copies were provided for them. One can see more clearly in this photograph the church. While the panoramic photograph is still before the Court, I will take Your Honours back to it briefly to make a point. Your Honours, my point is this: I indicate the church which has appeared on the panoramic photo on the video, and I indicate again the position of Lukavica barracks in which the accused had his office. And I make the point that it is a relatively short distance from his office to the source of fire for sniping which was carried out on Dobrinja throughout the indictment period. I anticipate that evidence will establish these propositions. I turn now to a brief reference to the relevant law. First I make the point that although the battle was often popularly referred to as a siege, it was not necessarily a siege in the way that term is understood militarily or in international law, and it is irrelevant to the issues in this case to make such a determination. Ultimately, this case is not about why the campaign in Sarajevo was fought. It is about how it was conducted. Indeed, this is the first case before this Tribunal with an explicit, indeed exclusive, focus upon the conduct of hostilities, and in particular, the scope of a military commander's obligation to protect civil life during armed combat. Since the confrontation lines at some points traversed urban areas, we can assume that there were many legitimate military targets within the city confines. Consequently, the Prosecution does not argue that the overall military campaign in Sarajevo was unlawful or that many attacks which took place during the indictment period did not comprise lawful combat activities. However, alongside and parallel to lawful combat operations, it is abundantly clear that civilians were unlawfully sniped and shelled on such a temporal and geographic scale as to constitute a deliberate campaign, which was conducted with the intent of striking terror into every civilian in the city. In the course of this trial, Your Honours will be referred to several baseline principles of international humanitarian law that are essential to a conduct of hostilities case but which have perhaps been less pertinent to many other cases previously adjudicated by this Tribunal. The first of these is the principle of distinction. This principle, the bedrock norm of international humanitarian law, obliges a military commander to differentiate, at all times, between civilian and military objects. He is obliged, at all times, to direct force only against military objectives. The definition of a military object is not entirely free from dispute. It is beyond contention, however, that it is only combatants who are lawful targets, and civilians are not. Similarly, buildings and objects used for military purposes may be targeted, whereas those used exclusively for civilian purposes may not. The second fundamental principle is that of proportionality, which obliges a military commander, when deciding whether to launch an attack against a legitimate military object, to undertake a particular type of calculus. He must evaluate whether the military advantage anticipated from the attack would be outweighed by the extent of civilian losses likely to result from it. A rational assessment of proportionality must be undertaken prior to and during the carrying out of the attacks. The overriding, governing principle in this regard is that of reasonableness in all the circumstances prevailing at the time. The Prosecution's case is that attacks carried out by forces under the command and control of the accused did not evidence a proportional character when assessed against notions of reasonableness which would be accepted by most responsible military commanders. The Prosecution notes that the present case confronts the Trial Chamber with a virtually unprecedented opportunity to elucidate principles to guide the practical application of these bedrock norms of international humanitarian law within modern armed combat. Simply stated, the doctrine that will be developed in this case will be of intense interest to, and may well form an operational litmus test for, responsible military forces worldwide. I turn now in particular to the counts. Six of the seven counts in the indictment against the accused are concerned specifically with the killing and wounding of civilians as a consequence of the campaign. The remaining count, which is the first in the indictment, is that the accused violated the laws or customs of war by inflicting terror and mental suffering on the civilian population of Sarajevo as a result of this campaign. I want to focus on this count. During the indictment period, the number of civilian casualties from the campaign ran into the thousands. However, in contrast to the other six counts, the victims of this crime were not limited to the Sarajevans who were killed or wounded but, as well, those who were terrorised as a result of the campaign. Had the accused wished to simply kill as many Sarajevans as possible, this was not the way to do it. He was equipped with the means to extract higher civilian casualty figures had that been his intention. The city was ringed with hills which contained hundreds of mortars, tanks, howitzers, rockets, and other artillery. It is apparent from the characteristics of the campaign over such a protracted period that the intention was not to kill as many civilians as possible, but rather to inculcate in each citizen the realisation that, so long as he or she remained in Sarajevo, they and their loved ones lived under an inescapable risk of death. As some witnesses will observe, a morbid fatalism overtook many civilians, expressed in the belief that it was futile to overly seek protection from mortars and the sniper's bullet. Death was unavoidable and would come regardless of what steps they took to prevent it. Soldiers expressed a feeling of greater security at the front line than when off-duty in the civilian areas, since at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. front they knew where danger lay, whereas elsewhere in the city, death could come from anywhere, at any time. As noted earlier, witnesses will be called to testify as to examples of the campaign. The scheduled incidents have been chosen to illustrate the range of everyday activities that civilians were engaged in at the time they were targeted. Beyond these scheduled incidents, those same witnesses will also testify about other incidents involving themselves and neighbours and friends and loved ones. A Sarajevan of this period typically knew many in his circle who had become victims of the campaign. In this fashion, a picture will emerge to the Trial Chamber of the pervasiveness of the campaign, its penetration of the fabric of Sarajevan society and the manner in which it delivered a sense of fear and terror far beyond its immediate victims. This unrelenting psychological stress exacted a horrific toll upon the well-being of the civilian populace, as reflected in attendances at psychiatric clinics during and after the conflict. Expert psychiatric evidence will be tendered to establish that the fear prevalent in Sarajevo during the indictment period was extreme, and far exceeded that which would be the normal and expected threshold of anxiety within armed conflict. This count is not concerned with the fear, and sometimes terror, which is inevitably felt by civilians who are caught up in an armed conflict, and no doubt was experienced by many civilians in Sarajevo. That is quite different in nature and degree from the terror which comes from the sure knowledge that you and your loved ones are in fact the intended target and there is nowhere to hide. The suffering of civilians was not merely an incidental by-product of the armed conflict in Sarajevo, but rather the intended consequence, and the actual effect, of the unlawful attacks perpetrated by the forces under the command and control of the accused. The inescapable conclusion in this regard is that the attacks against the civilians of Sarajevo during the indictment period were designed principally, even if not exclusively, to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo. Although it is well recognised that the deliberate and avoidable infliction of terror upon civilians as an objective is contrary to customary international law, this charge has not previously been adjudicated before any international judicial body. Both protocols additional to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 prohibit the infliction of terror upon a civilian population in the manner in which the accused did so, through forces under his command and control. Often the infliction of terror will be linked to the specific goals of the perpetrator. In this case, it meshed closely with the broader aims of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Clearly, had the terror imparted by the campaign weakened the civilians' morale or the political will of their government to a point that it capitulated, these aims would have been served. I will now turn my attention more particularly to the accused. He was born on 12 March 1943 in Golesa village, Banja Luka municipality, in the Republika Srpska Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a career soldier in the JNA, ultimately becoming commander of the 30th partisan Division. When the transition of the JNA into the army of the Republika Srpska, known as the VRS, occurred in May of 1992, he remained the commander of the Division, renamed the 30th infantry Division, and took part in a number of military operations within the operational area of the 1st Krajina Corps, including Jajce. He was appointed to the position of commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps by the president of the Republika Srpska Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, on the 31st of August, 1992. In November of the same year, he was promoted from Colonel to Major General. He remained commander until in August 1994 he was replaced, and shortly afterwards retired from active service by official decree on the 30th of September, 1994. Accordingly, the accused assumed command of the SRK as an experienced, professional soldier, fresh from active duty elsewhere. I turn now to the military doctrine. The military doctrine of the JNA effectively became that for the VRS, so the accused and his subordinates continued to operate under the doctrine with which he was familiar. The central tenet of that system was that each level of the structure acted under the orders of the superior. A system of regular briefings and distribution of written documentation carried these orders down the chain, and daily reporting brought back up to the superiors the results of the orders being carried out. In this manner, the corps acted as one integrated unit which carried out the orders of the supreme commander. According to that doctrine, the designated commander is vested with the authority to command his staff, subordinate units, institutions, and the personnel which comprise those bodies. It also establishes the responsibility of a commander, reiterating the concept that while a commander can delegate authority to subordinate officers, he remains responsible for the actions of those subordinates. Shortly following its formation, the Republika Srpska adopted key instruments of the international law of armed force. In so doing, it acknowledged the responsibility of each level of its military structure to respect international law which governs armed conflicts. The commander-in-chief of the VRS was the President, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Directly subordinate to him was General Ratko Mladic, who was the commander of the main staff of the VRS. Under the main staff command were the various corps of the VRS, including the SRK. I will now turn to the structure of the SRK. The Trial Chamber, I anticipate, will be concerned with where the units which conducted sniping and shelling fitted into that structure, and what disciplinary related measures and resources the accused had available to him. In relation to the term "sniping," it is important to understand that its use in this trial by the Prosecution is not confined to its strict military meaning, which is of a professional marksman utilizing a specialised rifle and scope. Instead, it is used in a broader sense, to include regular troops and the use of such armaments as hunting rifles, machine-guns, and anti-aircraft guns. In the video collage that you will view shortly, you will see a machine-gun in a sniper's nest overlooking the city, known amongst Sarajevans at the time as the Death Sower for that type of machine-gun, and this one, Your Honours will see, was fitted with a telescopic site, and also there was an anti-aircraft gun. I take you now to a diagram of the structure of the SRK. In taking you through this diagram, I want to highlight the chain of responsibility and how the artillery unit and sniper assets, as well as the regular troops and commanders were responsible to the accused. The essential structure of the SRK involved four levels of forces under the command of the accused. They were the accused's Main Staff at the corps headquarters, the brigades, the battalions, and the companies. There were nine brigades, about 2.000 soldiers in each. The battalions were at least 37 in number, about 200 to 700 soldiers in each, and finally, the companies comprised about 50 soldiers in each. As noted earlier, the central tenet of the VRS military doctrine was that each level operated under the orders of a superior. To put it another way, the 18.000 troops of the SRK were all ultimately responsible to the accused and acted on his orders. It was his job to know what was going on and to control the tempo and direction of combat activities. The accused would provide his operational objectives to say his Main Staff, who would develop a plan to put those objectives into effect. Orders were given to the implementation of the plan, which were then conveyed down the chain of command by daily briefings, and I indicate those lines of communication. Firstly, from the corps headquarters to the brigade headquarters, that is, the headquarters of the nine brigades. Those nine brigades ringed the city of Sarajevo. The briefings continued down the line from the brigades to the battalions, and then from the battalions to the companies. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honours, the lines of communication operated in both directions to carry back up the chain from the lowest rung of the structure, daily reports as to the implementation of the orders and other combat activities. This communication system is typical of that which applies to modern armed forces. It is a sensible means of ensuring that the forces, at even the lowest rung, understand what is required of them, and similarly, that their commander, in this case the accused, was thoroughly familiar with the activities of his forces. In this manner, the corps acted as one integrated formation, which carried out the orders of their overall commander, the accused. The diagram also demonstrates that within the Corps structure under his command, the accused had military police units, had he wanted to involve them in the investigation of allegations of unlawful conduct by his troops, and I indicate those. Firstly, a battalion of military police which was responsible directly under the corps headquarters, and in relation to the battalions, there were also military police companies. The diagram indicates those companies of which the Prosecution has evidence, the Prosecution anticipates that, in fact, each of the brigades would have had such military police units. Finally, in relation to the diagram, I point out the artillery and sniping units. The artillery units appear in red at various stages down the structure of the SRK. I come back to the first group of boxes that I indicated, and I invite the Trial Chamber to note that these artillery units were directly responsible to the accused's Main Staff. utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I leave the chart, I will briefly point out with the ELMO the relevant boxes in relation to artillery and sniping. It's now possible to see the red boxes which indicate the artillery units, and I'll point to those, and also the position in the structure where the snipers operated, and that is within the companies. The diagram also indicates the reporting and briefing structure, that is, briefings going down all the way to the company level and then reporting coming back up. I now turn to the responsibility of the accused pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. The Prosecution contends that the unlawful acts set forth in the indictment, and in particular, the schedules to the indictment, and those of similar character, were planned or ordered by the accused. Armies operate on principles of subordination and control. Acts which forces carry out in theatre are, over time, those which their commanders have ordered. When I say "ordered," I do not necessarily mean that the accused recorded these orders in writing. Indeed, given the blatant and serious degree of unlawfulness of the campaign, it would be surprising if written orders to this effect still exist, or were ever issued other than orally. The world was watching. The same could be said for the reports back up the structure to the Corps Commander, the accused. The temporal and geographic scale of the campaign demonstrates it to have been a deliberate campaign, which must have been the result of orders which came down from the highest level of command in the SRK, namely, from the accused. This campaign could not have continued for 22 months, throughout the city, on the other side of the confrontation lines from the accused, with the fire emanating from the SRK side of the confrontation lines, had it not been on the accused's orders. This sustained military operation did not just spontaneously occur. It was in place before he arrived and, as evidenced by the continued provision of ammunition alone by him to those who were carrying out the campaign, he chose to continue and sustain it. The fact that he was probably following orders from his superiors, General Mladic and President Karadzic, when issuing his orders to continue the campaign, does not relieve him of responsibility. In relation to Article 7(3) of the Statute, even if, extraordinary as it seems, the accused had not ordered the campaign, customary international law poses clear obligations upon commanders to prevent or punish the unlawful acts of subordinates. The accused did nothing to prevent the campaign from continuing, and did not punish those who were responsible. This cements his responsibility. Although in his pre-trial brief the accused denies it, there can be no doubt that he knew that unlawful acts were being committed by his subordinates, given the SRK reporting systems that were designed to inform him of daily combat activities right down to the lowest ranking commander. It is extraordinary to suggest that these attacks were not communicated up the chain, albeit not necessarily in written form, given their highly unlawful nature. Quite apart from the SRK reporting system, the accused and his senior subordinates in his corps headquarters were the frequent recipients of formal complaints about the shelling and sniping of civilians by numerous UN military observers and UN protection force senior officers, who had contact with him and his senior subordinates. And then there was the media. Journalists from around the world travelled to Sarajevo to report on the war. In his pre-trial brief, which was filed with this Chamber a few weeks ago, the accused claimed that no one in the SRK ever admitted to him that they were deliberately sniping civilians, and that the UN representatives never told him the identity of the perpetrators. The corollary, it seems, is that he felt it inappropriate to order an investigation until he was told the name of his soldier who pulled the trigger for a specific incident, or at least his specific unit, and therefore he did nothing. At a bare minimum, the accused was at least put on inquiry that crimes may have been committed by his subordinates, which obliged him to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. investigate further. Customary international law requires the Prosecution to prove only that the accused "had reason to know" of the acts of his subordinates. In relation to the deliberate sniping and shelling of civilians, at paragraph 2.47 of the Defence pre-trial brief, he said "he hadn't any knowledge of such events." And at paragraph 6.32, that he had "never received even a single report on any individual incident, and that he did not undertake an investigation regarding such an incident." Your Honours, during those two years that he commanded the SRK, the accused must have been the only person in the world who did not know of credible allegations that the residents of Sarajevo were being deliberately sniped and shelled on a daily basis from the hills surrounding the city. The hills which he controlled. All the more strange, when one considers evidence that he had a television in his office in his forward command post at Lukavica barracks. All he had to do was turn it on. One witness will tell you that in 1993, not surprisingly, he saw a television running in the office of the accused's liaison officer. It was tuned to CNN. The powers of a Corps Commander of the Republika Srpska army as to punishment are extensive. Expert testimony will identify the precise scope and nature of the accused's responsibility in-theatre and will pinpoint exactly what types of measures would have been within his powers. These included the ability to remove offending persons from front-line positions, to issue orders, to effect improvements with levels of training, to amend Rules the Engagement, and to initiate disciplinary measures. The accused admits in his pre-trial brief he did not undertake any such or similar measures in relation to any of the incidents detailed in the schedules to the indictment, or others of a similar character. Finally, Your Honours, I will show a short collage of video clips. It takes approximately 8 minutes and 40 seconds, taken before and during the indictment period, up to approximately spring of 1993. I do so in order to demonstrate more vividly than words could some of the anticipated evidence I have alluded to during my opening. On the video, the state of the foliage and the clothing being worn by people indicates the seasons and thus whether the footage was taken broadly in the summer months of 1992, or after the accused assumed command of the SRK in early September of that year. A brief explanatory note prefaces each segment. It starts with footage of civilians attempting to avoid sniper fire as they run across an intersection which was exposed to SRK positions, early in the conflict. The second clip is of the same intersection during the indictment period, by which time anti-sniping barricades, in the form of shipping containers, had been placed on it. Thereafter follows general footage of civilians attempting it avoid sniper fire, sometimes unsuccessfully, and footage of civilians collecting water and firewood, footage of the after math of three scheduled shelling incidents and the burial of the dead in Dobrinja, in a plot of land adjacent to a car park because do to so in a cemetery was unthinkable given the campaign of shelling of funeral processions. The video illustrates, in particular, the terror that was communicated not just to those who were unable to dodge the sniper's bullet or the shells, but to those who lived and witnesses what happened to their fellow Sarajevans. It conveys a sense as to how they were the targets, even though they were not hit, of the intention to inflict terror. Thank you. Perhaps that video might be shown.
