utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Starting from the east, there are the municipalities of Pale, Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, Hadzici, Ilijas, Trnovo, and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of those municipalities make up the actual urban part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The urban part consists of four municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you just name which four are those urban municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo, and Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I'd like you, please, to tell the Judges a little about Sarajevo in its pre-war condition and the pre-war lifestyle of the city. Can you tell us firstly, please, something about the commercial life of Sarajevo before the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo, as a town, dates back 500 years, when it was first established at the crossroads of roads as a commercial centre. After the Second World War, and especially after the winter Olympic games in 1984, in addition to being the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it also became a cultural and economic centre of the former Yugoslavia. Four out of the six largest civil engineering and consulting companies of the former Yugoslavia were based in Sarajevo. In the music life, cultural life, university life, and in many other aspects, Sarajevo was a prominent centre independent of Belgrade and Zagreb, another of the main centres of the former Yugoslavia, in which all its inhabitants lived in harmony, regardless of their religious or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To move to that, Mr. Kupusovic, how large was the population of Sarajevo by, say, the year 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Half a million inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us which or what ethnic groups might have composed that population?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: About 40 per cent of the population was Muslim, about 32 per cent Serbs, and 8 per cent Croats, and the rest mixed marriages and people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, people who considered themselves to be citizens of Yugoslavia or members of other ethnic groups constituted the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe in a little more detail the relationships that there were between the ethnic groups within the city.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that relationships were harmonious; in fact, there wasn't any part of town or any institution or any company which was dominated by members of only one ethnic group. Simply, citizens considered themselves fellow citizens, and the small differences that existed in religious terms were not an obstacle. They exchanged visits for religious holidays, such as Bajram, family celebrations, and other festivities. So as a citizen of Sarajevo, I can assert that it was the most cosmopolitan town in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the relationships between the members of the city council at the political level, say towards the latter part of 1990 and into 1991?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In the city council or city parliament, there were 120 elected deputies or members, and they belonged to different parties. There were seven parties who had won enough votes to be represented in the parliament, and relationships were very good. As members of the town assembly, we sought to develop a new multiparty spirit. For instance, the option of social democracy, liberalism, the greens, all the various options, regardless of the three national parties, which also had their representatives in the assembly, but not one of them had a majority. The party I belonged to had the largest number of deputies, that is, the SDA, which had 30 or 32 per cent of seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to three national parties, what precisely do you mean? Does that have any reference to ethnic groups at all?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the members, or one could even say almost all the members of the Serbian Democratic Party were Serbs. Of the Croatian Democratic Union were Croats, and also the majority of members of the Party of Democratic Action were Muslims or Bosniaks. The other parties were definitely multi-ethnic. Not a single ethnic group dominated in those parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, were any of these political parties known simply by a set of initials? And if so, could you tell us which of these parties may have been known just by their initials?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the parties had their initials. The three most important ones were the SDA, that is, the Party of Democratic Action; the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union; and the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, headed by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your political career, did you continue in public office after and throughout the 1990s, up to, say, 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the town assembly from the elections in 1990 up to 1994, when I was elected town mayor of Sarajevo, and I performed those duties until 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kupusovic, just as to the pre-war situation in Sarajevo, were there any particular features of the city that aroused particular affection or sentiment amongst its people, anything they were especially proud of?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: All the inhabitants of Sarajevo were then, and still are, proud in particular of the old town centre, where, in an area of 400 metres you have the Orthodox church, the Gasi Husref Bey mosque, the largest mosque in the Balkans, then the Catholic cathedral and the old Jewish synagogue. In addition, the people of Sarajevo are particularly proud of the facilities that were built just before the Olympic Games, which transformed a town that developed in the 1950s and 1960s under socialism and communism into a modern European city. Thanks to those buildings, and also thanks to a new infrastructure, water supply, electricity, gas supply, the facilities that were built in the 1980s sponsored by the need for the Olympic Games.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned as well, what was the system, the public transport system in the city at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, in addition to the trams, which date back to the nineteenth century, the first trams, in fact, that were introduced in the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, trolley buses were introduced, and of course there were buses for transport all over town, so that the city transport system functioned extremely well from the Olympics right through until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kupusovic, whereabouts were you living in 1992, the beginning of the year?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in the district called Dobrinja, which is close to the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you always lived in that district?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's a housing settlement built for the needs of the athletes and journalists for the Olympic Games, and I moved into a new apartment there in 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so where were you in fact living at the beginning of April of 1992? In Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Dobrinja, very close to Sarajevo's airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, what effect did any events in the former Yugoslavia have on the minds and daily life of the people in Sarajevo towards the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: When the crisis started of the break-up of the structures of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, first with Slovenia, followed by Croatia, the vast majority of people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the very large majority of the people of Sarajevo believed that a peaceful solution would be found after all to that crisis and that the war from Croatia would not spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sarajevo itself. In fact, on January 1st, 1992, a peace agreement was signed in Sarajevo between the rump Yugoslavia and Croatia whereby that stage of the war in Croatia, when Vukovar, Dubrovnik, and other towns were particularly badly damaged, ended. We believed that nothing like that could ever happen to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially not in Sarajevo, in which, before and even after that, the people were absolutely in favour of peace and a peaceful settlement of the crisis rather than what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And faced with that situation, did anything change as regards those amicable relations in the early months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't change a lot, but nevertheless, after the referendum that took place on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, at which the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to declare whether they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wished to remain within the rump Yugoslavia, that is, together with Serbia, or whether they wanted to have an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, some members of the SDS set up the first checkpoints in Sarajevo to demonstrate their rejection of the results of the referendum which later on resulted in the recognition and the actual independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was officially recognised by the European union, there were fresh barricades in the night between the 5th and 6th of April, but our colleague deputies in the town assembly, that is, colleagues, members on behalf of the SDS, claimed that they had nothing to do with it, that they were not involved and that this was being done by groups that were out of control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to ascertain what the purpose of these barricades was?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the barricades, according to what the president and vice-president of the SDS were saying, was to express their disagreement, that is, the disagreement of the SDS as a party, but at the level of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the results of that referendum. So that as these barricades lasted -- were up for a few hours, that is, a limitation on freedom of movement, there were occasional shootings, but all we could do was guess as to what the purpose was, as a kind of test, an exercise on the part of the people who were prepared to engage in such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the mood of the population at large when these events were going on?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The reaction of the population was to organise peaceful actions to remove the barricades, and that is what happened. For the first time in March, and a second time in April, when large crowds of people consisting of men, women, and children, headed towards those barricades, and the people who were camouflaged with caps and socks over their faces who were manning those barricades, were removed. Similarly, on the 5th of April, an enormous mass of people from all over Bosnia came to Sarajevo to demonstrate peacefully against those who had put up those barricades, and to urge them to remove them, which indeed happened, of course with some sporadic shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupusovic, had there been any form of military stationed in or situated in Sarajevo prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war in Sarajevo, the Yugoslav People's Army had several barracks in the town itself and several facilities in the environs of the town. The only military in Sarajevo was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say where precisely they were located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The largest barracks was the Marsal Tito barracks in the very centre of town. It is a very large compound in area, and in the old part of town and in new districts, there were several smaller barracks and facilities for the training of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And generally, what were the activities of the JNA soldiers in the city prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew from Croatia and Slovenia, much of the troops and armaments arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and much of that in Sarajevo. And the number of patrols increased considerably. They were passing through town in APCs and in other vehicles, which had an adverse effect on the citizens, and they saw it as a demonstration of military might.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there at that point. What were the activities, then, prior to that sort of period on the part of the JNA. I mean, did they -- how much did you see of them in the town and what sort of activities did they have in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1990s, for instance, the military was in town and around town, but relations were fine. There were local, amateur, cultural, and arts societies, together with the soldiers. The soldiers would go out when they were on leave, to go to coffee shops and various cultural institutions, and relations were quite amicable between the soldiers and the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so generally, what indeed was the attitude of the people towards the JNA and the purpose that the JNA were serving?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The attitude towards the JNA before the war in Croatia was extremely favourable. After the war, in Slovenia and Croatia, this attitude became more neutral. Yes, they are our army, but because of certain actions which did not meet with approval, it had become to Serbianised, as we used to say, because too many Slovenes and Croats had left the army, so that it was no longer the army of all the peoples of Yugoslavia, but still it was considered to be a neutral force which would protect the constitutional order and peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a few minutes ago that you saw, after the events of the trouble in Croatia, that the JNA increased in numbers of men and weapons in the vicinity of Sarajevo. Could you tell us a little bit more, please, about what you witnessed as to the return of these JNA troops into the city.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was common knowledge that the number of soldiers and that large numbers of soldiers and weapons were moved from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in Sarajevo we saw images on television of increased activity by the JNA around Sarajevo. JNA commanders said these were regular activities to protect the town. Some citizens believed this, but others expressed fear. They said, "Who is the JNA protecting us from by setting up guns and other weapons around Sarajevo?" I myself, because I lived in Dobrinja, and there was a crossroads leading to Trebevic from my house, and I saw that that part of the road was closed off for civilians and that personnel carriers, tanks, and guns had been set up on the Mojmilo tank, which was on the other side of Dobrinja, in the direction of town, so that soldiers were everywhere, and one did not really understand who they were protecting the citizens from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference to Mojmilo tank. Can you explain, please, to the Court the place you're actually referring to. What is Mojmilo tank?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Mojmilo reservoir is the biggest water reservoir in Sarajevo, into which water is pumped and then redistributed to smaller pumping stations for the water supply of the town. This is on a hill overlooking the airport, the new part of town, and Dobrinja, which is close to the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that guns had been set up on that location, can you give us a description of what type of guns they appeared to be?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not an expert on this. They were guns with long barrels, but I can't say anything more about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. So you were referring to the other events that had been occurring around the beginning of April. Was there any particularly significant event on the 6th of April of 1992 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the 6th of April is the day of liberation of Sarajevo from World War II, and it was always celebrated as a holiday in the town. And there was to be a ceremonial session of the city assembly, which was not held, because in the night from the 5th to 6th of April, barricades were set up, and only some of the people were able to make their way to the assembly. I arrived in a taxi at a barricade, then crossed on foot, took another taxi to the next barricade, and that's how I managed to get through to the assembly. I didn't have any special problems except that I couldn't use my own car or public transport. The barricades were manned by masked people, and their role was unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say they were masked people. Was there any other way that you might have identified who they were or who they represented?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. They had socks over their heads and they were not wearing military uniforms, so they didn't look like soldiers or policemen. They were armed and that they were manning the barricade. But they were not preventing people from passing by the barricade on foot, but you couldn't pass through in a vehicle. We knew, however, that they were members of the SDS because on television we saw negotiations between President Izetbegovic and Karadzic, the president of the Serbian party, on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. removal of the barricades, and the mediator was a representative of the UN in Sarajevo. And this is what happened, actually. On the following day the barricades were removed and peace was negotiated, and it was said that barricades would no longer be erected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after that incident and the barricades were removed, what was the position in the city? What was the situation?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout April, the situation was tense. At a high level in the police, efforts were needed find a solution, but there was sporadic shooting in town. There were incidents which instilled fear and made people afraid. However, everything continued to function. Public transport, utilities, people went to work. And our slogan was that by working, we were fighting for peace, because this was the way to prevent a possible war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have referred to a number of incidents and shootings. Can you give the Chamber any facts relating to any of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: When the peace rally was held, in front of the assembly of the socialist Republic, or rather, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was already called, and the Executive Council, that is, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rally was broken up by shots coming from the Holiday Inn, a nearby hotel, and several people were wounded. Later on, when the peace demonstrators set out towards the police school, that was where the first civilian casualty occurred, on the bridge on the other side of the assembly, leading to the part of town where the police school is. Throughout the month there were a few peaceful days, followed by days when there was sporadic shooting from the smaller barracks around town, and the shooting was actually done by people who were unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that first instance of the first civilian casualty shot on a bridge, can you give us any more details about that? Do you know anything about the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a female student in Sarajevo who came from Dubrovnik. She was studying in Sarajevo. Her name was Suada Omerovic, she was the first victim of the war in Sarajevo, so the bridge is today named after her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did that event therefore have a strong significance in the mind of the people at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It did. She was a young girl studying in Sarajevo who wanted peace, and in a way, people felt obliged by her death. They saw that more such casualties could happen if people did not leave off weapons and try to find peaceful solutions for the misunderstandings in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone ascertain or find out how she came to be shot, where the shot came from or who did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The police established that the shots were fired by the bodyguards of Radovan Karadzic. That's what was published in the newspapers. I of course have no personal knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Did you have any knowledge as to the whereabouts of those bodyguards of Dr. Karadzic at the time of the shooting? Where were they? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: They were on two floors of the Holiday Inn hotel, and in other nearby buildings. But this is where the SDS headquarters was. After the rallies and after this event, they moved to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so after that particular event on the 6th of April, how did things progress in the city in terms of the atmosphere and the general air of whether it was calm or tensions rising?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The tensions mounted because many more soldiers were moving in and around town, and the citizens tried to carry on with their normal lives and to oppose the militarisation of the town and the military activities in this way. They felt that all this was pointless and that it only increased the danger of new incidents. There were incidents throughout April: Shootings, woundings, and other events where people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the JNA troops in the city of Sarajevo doing while these incidents were going on? In fact, were they involved in any of them?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA forces played the role of a neutral mediator, separating, as they said, the opposing sides. But there were no opposing sides. In fact, there was only the SDS, the guards, the lads who were the SDS militia, and then there were the JNA soldiers. There were also groups of young men in Sarajevo, citizens patrolling the streets without any weapons, patrolling the streets and the entrances to residential buildings, to watch out for crime, for drunken soldiers, and reserve soldiers who committed crimes around town. So tensions mounted, and at a higher political level, they kept changing ideas about how to preserve Yugoslavia peacefully or else how to make a new political agreement in order for the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia to develop into a peaceful community of federal states or confederation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I'm intending to have a short break of approximately 20 minutes. Would this be a proper moment to start this break, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As convenient as any, Your Honour. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a short break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, could you please proceed. First, of course, we need the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes. As soon as he's in court, I will of course proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher please -- is he there or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, just before the break we were talking a little about the activities of the JNA at that time, at the beginning of April, but can you tell us something about events in and around Sarajevo airport that might have occurred shortly before then?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army took over control of the airport from the civil administration of the airport, and already in March and April it had full control of the airport and all the air traffic at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the air traffic at the airport include still civil traffic or was it exclusively military at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There was a very pronounced military traffic. As I lived nearby, I saw planes landing and taking off. But there were also civilian airplanes landing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as we progress through the month of April after these particular events, particularly around the 6th, can you tell us sort of how events went in the city as that month went on?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean. I have already spoken about the heightening tensions and the efforts of citizens to maintain normalcy of life in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Probably my fault. I don't think it was a very precise question. I'll ask you something more precise and more on the point. Was there any time after that that the JNA became more militarily involved with any groups or other people with some sort of conflict in the city during April?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a number of what the JNA commanders called exercises by the JNA, in town and around town, which provoked fear among the population and an increase in tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any time at which the JNA became involved in actual shooting incidents with anybody?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There were shooting incidents, as I have already mentioned, but I did not know, nor did other people know, who was doing the shooting. I, for instance, remember a statement by General Kukanjac, who was commander of the garrison, or the area of Sarajevo, that when citizens were saying that it was the JNA that were shooting, he said that the JNA was a force that would not trample on an ant, that it would maintain the peace. But there were constant exercises and movements by the military and a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heightening of tensions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever a time at which there was an open confrontation between people in the vicinity of the Tito barracks during the month of April?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There were some incidents. From the barracks outside, but it could not really be called a confrontation. It was simply a mirroring of events that took place in Capljina and Mostar, where there were even more troops than in Sarajevo, relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, how had relations developed between the delegates within your city assembly? Was it still as harmoniously conducted, as you have previously described, or was there a change?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There were no particular changes. We would meet. In those days I was already president of the deputy club of my party, and those presidents met in an effort to ease tension and to preserve the functions of the city. And the president of the SDS deputy club also took part in those meetings. His name was Bozo Popara, and of course the president of the SDS was Karadzic, but Popara was president of the SDS for the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- you've described obviously how tensions had heightened and there were problems. Had there been any kind of shift or change in the population or any movement of population by this point, in April?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A part of the population, maybe a couple of thousand, in March and April, left on JNA planes and in other they left the town. These were mostly family members of JNA officers who were serving in town, who were living in town, but also other citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any particular ethnic group that saw more of its citizens leaving Sarajevo than others?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, as the officers were mostly Serbs, so maybe there were more Serbs who were leaving the town, but others were leaving too, Croats and Muslims. They were sending their wives and small children. Some were either to the Adriatic coast or to some other destination, believing they would stay there for a month or two, until the situation calmed down. That was what everyone told me who had sent their families either to the Adriatic, to Croatia, or to Germany. That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at about that time, let us say mid-April, was there any particular action that was taken by the city assembly perhaps on or about the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: As the assembly could not meet on the 6th of April because of the barricades, which we have discussed, then a limited number of people, the leaders of the parties who had deputies in the city assembly, met in an effort to find a solution for the city itself to ensure peace and further development. On the 17th of April, a statement was signed which was made public in the local newspapers by the presidents of the deputy clubs, to the effect that we wished to preserve the assets of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you there, sir? I apologise. I do have a document I would like to have shown to this witness at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Does the usher have the document to present to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This gives me opportunity, Mr. Blaxill, perhaps to make a proposal as far as tendering of exhibits in evidence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I don't propose to tender this as an exhibit. The reality is that this is a document of a very brief nature and is germane really to the main text of the witness's evidence. I was proposing to invite him to read it into the record of the transcript and not, in fact, tender the document. That being said, it has been prepared as an aid to Your Honours and to my learned friends, and indeed has been translated into both English and French to assist in that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have received a copy, Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we haven't received that document, Mr. President, but I think last time we wanted to focus in particular on translation problems. And I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to say that when the witness said "a little more," and I didn't see that reflected in the transcript. So we're going to have these problems, and how should we react when a statement made in one language doesn't appear in an exact translation in another language? I'm not quite sure what we are referring to, so I can't say regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would concentrate rather than on this document at this moment, and perhaps if there are any problems as far as corrections to the translations are concerned, we'll deal with that at a later stage and to find a way to solve that problem as far as we can. But as regards this document, I do understand that we haven't had a copy, the Defence hasn't had a copy, but we get it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In point of fact, Your Honour, that is not quite so. We have copies for distribution that were tendered this morning, and my learned friend in fact received it on the 26th of November. It was handed to Madam Pilipovic by a colleague of mine, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I have to apologise. Shortly before this Court hearing started, I was provided with a copy, and you've got a copy as well? I see it's a document which says in English "statement made by a representative." That's the document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence has got a copy as well? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just as an observation, Your Honour, I think you'll find any comments about translation will be resolved, because as you read it into the record, our interpreters here will be translating formally to the Court in both French and English. Could the document be handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, could you look at that document, and do you recognise it? Can you say what it is?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document that was published in the local newspapers, a statement by representatives of parliamentary parties in the city assembly of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the contents of that document into the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the document is headed "The town is indivisible." [As interpreted] "At a meeting in the assembly of the town of Sarajevo held on the 19th of April, 1992, in the work of which representatives of all parliamentary parties whose deputies constitute the town assembly participated, and it was chaired by the president of the City Assembly, Muhamed Kresevljakovic, a joint statement was adopted and signed: "On behalf of the citizens of Sarajevo, no one from the town or the Republic," and the implication is to Bosnia and Herzegovina, "or Europe has the right to negotiate any divisions of Sarajevo. "The town of Sarajevo, with a history of more than 500 years long of joint life as a multicultural, multi-confessional and multi-ethnic community, is indivisible. "In the town of Sarajevo, we are defended a modern European civil concept of life. "Sarajevo is the capital of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all human rights and freedoms are respected in it, due to which we hereby state that no one has the right to jeopardise the lives of people, peace, and the material property of citizens and the cultural and historical and natural heritage of Sarajevo." The signatories are Miodrag Jankovic, the Alliance of Reformist Forces, a party; Bozidar Popara, the Serbian Democratic Party; Tarik Kupusovic, the Party of Democratic Action, or the SDA; Anto Zelic, the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ; Slobodan Primorac, the SDP, the Socialist Democratic Party; Esad Afgan, the MBO, the Muslim Bosniak Organisation; Nijaz Nurkovic, Liberals; Ibrahim Spahic, DSS, the Democratic Party of Socialists; and Muhamed Kresevljakovic, the town mayor of Sarajevo. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So all the presidents of the urban part of the party signed, including the SDS, Bozidar Popara, and I who at the time was the president of the SDA club of deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There is just one issue of translation at this point, Your Honours, although it's probably of little significance, but the Alliance of Reformist Forces has been referred to as the party of Miodrag Jankovic, but I had a translation of the Serbian Radical Party. Would that be the same thing or is that an error?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Alliance of Reformist Forces, a party that came into effect a year or 18 months before this time we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which alphabet is that notice prepared, and in which alphabet was it published, Mr. Kupusovic?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any significance to your having had it published in Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. The newspapers would be published one day in Cyrillic and one day in Latin script, or some newspapers in Latin, some in Cyrillic. So we had the technical facilities to publish in both scripts, and the emphasis was on the equality of scripts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that both scripts were in use, both the Cyrillic and the Latin. So just it happens to be a coincidence that it was published in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've talked about the incidents and incidents of violence that occurred in April. Was there a time when that changed and the situation became rather predominantly more violent, there were greater incidents and shooting?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In April, the situation was under constant tension, and on the 2nd of May, of course, the situation exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what actually happened to explain what you mean by "the situation exploded."

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: A column of APCs and tanks was heading towards the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the same time, the army centre in downtown Sarajevo, close to the Presidency building, was being evacuated, and there was shooting, an explosion, as I said, which provoked setting light to trams, killings, and it was then, in fact, that the war really started in Sarajevo, this lengthy apathy of life in town under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Kupusovic, whose column of APCs and tanks were these? Who was using them?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were heading, you say, for the Presidency. Where did they actually end up?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: They were stopped at the bridge in front of the town assembly, which is right close to the Presidency building, and they were stopped, in fact, by the guards of the Presidency and the town assembly, that is, units of the regular police, so that fighting occurred. The assumption was, of course, since negotiations were underway at the same time in Lisbon on the implementation of the results of the referendum, that that was in fact an attempted coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after these APCs were stopped, what happened? Did they remain there? Did they withdraw? What happened to that armoured column?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Several were destroyed, and the others withdrew. But at the same time several trams were set on fire, several cars and shooting occurred in town and that marked the beginning of the war conflict in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say, sir, who were the other people involved in these incidents you refer to as unrest and riots? Were there any particular groups involved?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from police units and units of the reserve police units who were actually protecting the Presidency building as a symbol of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Hercegovina, there were several groups of self-organised young men who were assisting them. These groups called themselves Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you -- you say there were groups calling themselves Bosna, did they represent any particular political party or any particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No they were young men from Sarajevo who felt that there was impending trouble and there were several hundred of them, several groups who were assisting the police in maintaining the law and order and civility in Sarajevo in March and April, but they were in civilian clothes. They were just citizens acting together with the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened after those particular incidents? What then happened in the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: After that the town was exposed to very heavy shelling. A couple of days later the Bascarsija was set alight, the national and university libraries, the railway station, the post office and many key buildings in town were heavily shelled and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date or the approximate date that that shelling began?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: This started already on the 2nd or 3rd of May and went on for several weeks, with interruptions, of course, went every day or every other day we experienced shocks. Zetar [phoen] was destroyed, the Olympic Sports Hall, that the railway station had gone, that many apartments buildings had burned or several floors of those buildings and several apartments, and this went on during the following weeks and months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you just a little more closely about that. When the first shells landed upon the city, can you say the areas in which they landed? Were they specific areas, or what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The buildings that I mentioned are scattered all over town, so one could not identify a particular part of town being targeted, except for the buildings themselves, that were symbols of the town and were essential for its functioning, like the post office, the railway stations, the Zetar sports hall, and similar such facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your recollection, at that time, were those buildings the only ones that received shell hits, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, several apartment buildings were destroyed, many high-rises had apartments burning. The part of town where I had lived until then, Dobrinja, right close to the airport, where the JNA was, half of those apartments were set alight at the very beginning, and I found that out from a neighbour who happened to be there. Whereas when these things were happening on the 2nd of May, I happened to be in the centre of town, staying at my wife's parents' house. Twenty days later, the telephone lines were cut because the post office was set alight, so you could not use the phone any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Kupusovic, that you lived in Dobrinja at that time. Were you able to make a return to your home?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. About a quarter past 11.00, when this fighting around the Presidency started, I happened to be in the street, and when I heard the shooting, I was with my children, so I went back to my in-laws' place, and in instead of going to -- by tram to Dobrinja, where we were planning to go, the tram stopped and we spent the following two and a half months in that apartment with my in-laws, because we couldn't go to Dobrinja any more. And when we called up our next-door neighbour in Dobrinja, we learnt from her that we had nowhere to go, because the apartment had been set on fire, and there was also no transportation. Everything was under blockade. It was not possible to move around town. And from the Marsal Tito barracks, which was on the way, there was shooting going from the barracks in all directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was occupying the Marsal Tito barracks at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you refer to shooting, can you tell the kind of shooting it was in terms of the weapons? Was this small firearms or was it big guns type shooting from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: From the barracks there was side arms, rifle fire, and also the so-called Zolja, the hand-held rocket launchers for armoured vehicles, but they were also used to destroy apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say the kind of areas that came under fire from the Tito barracks when that shooting started? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: All parts of town were targeted, which could be reached from the barracks. So there was shooting in all four directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effects did this shooting from the Tito barracks have upon the ability of the civilian population to function within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the barracks is in the centre of town. It is a large compound. And due to this fire coming from the barracks, these two parts of town -- there was no communication between the two parts of town on each side of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "on each side of the barracks," are you talking of north to south or east to west?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: All four sides: East/west and north/south. Because the two main roads are on each side of the barracks. They couldn't be used. And also, north south, the north/south direction could not be used because of the shooting coming from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any people hit by that shooting that was coming from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The television was still operational. There was electricity, and we repeatedly saw images or news reports about killings or wounding of children, women, or men who happened to be in the line of fire of people, I suppose, soldiers, in the barracks who were doing the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say again: How long did it go on that there was this shooting from Tito barracks out into the streets of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: This went on for several weeks, until the point in time when it was agreed at the negotiations that the JNA should move to Serbia, that is, what was left of Yugoslavia, when the barracks was evacuated. So that would be about a month and a half later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any form or group of people who were actually opposing the JNA, fighting with them at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In the former republics, the socialist republics of the former Yugoslavia, there was the Territorial Defence as a local organisation, that is, of the Republic, and already at the beginning of May, I think officially in mid-May, it was mobilised. And together with the reserve police force and the police force and the self-organised groups of young men, who all later became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of that army, those were in fact the force that opposed and that sought to preserve the town and protect the citizens from these attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, while the JNA was in those barracks and this fighting was going on, what about the shelling of the city? Was that continuing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, the city was shelled, mostly from positions around Sarajevo, but also from these barracks which were still under JNA control in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did any -- to your recollection, did any shells hit the JNA barracks while they were there, at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that any shell hit the barracks, but those young men in the police didn't have the weapons with which to shell. There were no heavy weapons on their side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether any of the shells coming in from the outside of the city hit the Tito barracks at that time while the JNA were there?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: That was the same army, both outside town and in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact personally see the Tito barracks buildings during this period, or did you not go near that particular area?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to the immediate vicinity of the barracks because it was impossible to reach it, but the apartment which was behind the Holiday Inn hotel, we could see the walls of the barracks, compound. It can be seen virtually from any part of town, because it is a very large compound of buildings, a complex of buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so from those observations that you were able to make at the time, if you just think back, Mr. Kupusovic, do you recall seeing any noticeable damage to those barracks during that period, while the JNA were there in May?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what had happened at this time to your city assembly, now that you had these conditions in which to try and function?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The city assembly had been unable to meet since April, so we did not have a quorum and were unable to make decisions. Under the legislation that was then in force, the Presidency of the town took over the functions of the city assembly, and it is these signatures here that it consisted of: The mayor, the deputy mayor, and the commander of the civil defence, and the chief of the town police. It started operating in June, because in May it was still not possible to move around. The situation was totally unsafe. And from early June until January or February 1994, the Presidency of the town took on the functions of the town assembly as the highest authority of civilian government in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I will at some future point be asking you a bit more about that, Mr. Kupusovic, but at the moment: Were you in fact a member of that body, the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So after we have this change in civilian administration, you have made reference, I believe, to a time when the JNA left the Tito barracks. Could you just describe briefly the circumstances that led to that and where they went?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: When Bosnia and Herzegovina became a member of the UN as a sovereign state, negotiations were held by people at higher political levels, and it was agreed that the JNA should move out of Bosnia and Herzegovina and thus from Sarajevo and the Marsal Tito barracks. They moved out, and this was monitored by the UN. They were to leave behind their heavy weapons for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to take with them only their personal weapons. When they were moving out, some of them stayed in Grbavica, which is a part of town on the other side of the river. And as I said, we still had TV broadcasts, and of course we watched both Belgrade and Zagreb TV. And young men who had been doing their military service in the JNA really did go back to their homes and their families, but evidently the largest part of the JNA - officers, soldiers, and weapons - stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, around Sarajevo, and they were simply transformed into the army of Karadzic's Serbs, or later on, the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so at that time, were any areas established or locations in the city established where we could refer to them, say, as front lines, occupied by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: In April, May, early July, no lines had yet been established. We couldn't call those lines. The urban areas where people lived were patrolled by reserve policemen and the units of the Territorial Defence and volunteers from the houses and flats where people lived. I don't remember the exact date when a state of war was declared and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formally established and general mobilisation was announced. In Sarajevo, this meant setting up an army to defend the town. It was only in September or October that one could speak of lines being established when trenches began to be dug by the town, which was under siege from all sides, and these trenches were the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. So in May, the situation you've described clearly did not lead to any settled confrontation. You have referred to mobilisations. What in fact happened, and when was that initiated, to try and mobilise a defence force?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued a call for mobilisation, saying that able-bodied young men were to report to the municipal mobilisation bodies, and that is how the organisation of the army began. Its first commander was the commander of the Territorial Defence, who, during the former Yugoslavia and during the time of the JNA, when they controlled the town, had been the Territorial Defence commander. He expressed loyalty to the government of sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. Later on, of course, there were changes, and the mobilisation was carried out according to city districts and municipalities, and people responded, but there were no weapons or uniforms, or there were very small amounts. And there was a big depot containing weapons and equipment for the Territorial Defence on the edge of the town, and this was moved overnight by the JNA. It was moved to another location, where it could not be used to arm and equip the regular army of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was in Faletici, where this depot used to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your city Presidency have any role in the military aspect of the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have described that during this period -- we have had a description of shelling of the city. Can you say whether these shellings resulted in human casualties?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, we appear to have an indication there was no interpretation of my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was the answer to the question, as far as I can see, it's "A. No interpretation." I didn't hear any answer pronounced by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I thought he said "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a very short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I ask the question again for clarity on the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, did your presidency have any role in the military aspect of the defence of city of Sarajevo? Could you answer that question again, please, sir, for our records here.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: No. It had no role in the military aspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just before that, Mr. Kupusovic, I had asked you whether there had been any human casualties as a result of the shelling of the city that had commenced then and been going for a little while during May of 1992. Can you tell me if you know that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were numerous casualties. We could hear ambulances, the sirens of ambulances driving the wounded to hospital. There were ten or fifteen casualties every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall or do you know whether these casualties were civilian casualties or were people who were engaged in some kind of active hostilities?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians. Also, there were some policemen or members of these groups defending the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Kupusovic, of any kind of proportion between the two as to which civilian or these other groups had the greater casualties at that time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: 95 per cent of the victims were civilians, and only a few per cent were reserve policemen and other members of the city defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of those casualties, were they only casualties of the shelling of the city, or were there any other ways in which they were being killed?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of shooting from infantry weapons, and citizens started calling these sniper shots, people at crossroads or in the streets were wounded or killed in this way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what initially did the citizens do to try and protect themselves, say, when they were at crossroads or at other places in the city as regards this shooting that they refer to as sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning after the 2nd of May, most citizens stayed in their basements. They were afraid to go out. They had to go out, however, in order to get bread or to run an errand or see a friend or visit someone who was wounded, and they either had to make detours through narrow streets where there was less danger from the sniping, or they had to run across these places, risking being shot, because there was no other way of crossing from one part of the street, one side of the street to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to explore just a little more about the actual style of this shooting. I mean, was this a situation of people who were very close to some kind of actual military group, or were these shots of a different type, at longer range or unseen?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: People crossing the streets or moving around, these people were all civilians. The shooting was from Mount Trebevic, overlooking Sarajevo, from the wood, or in other parts of town, from wooded areas around the town. In mid-May, I personally waited for half an hour with my daughter to cross the street. I kept thinking whether I should go back or cross. And when I thought that the shooting had stopped, we ran across, and on our way back we looked for a way around, a detour, in order to go back. And then, of course, my wife was very angry because I had risked my own life and my daughter's life. However, later on, she did the same thing herself, because there was no other way. You couldn't keep on sitting in the basement waiting for the situation to end. You had to organise your family, your life, under these risky conditions, among all the sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Kupusovic, was this, therefore, a regular occurrence that there was sniping of this nature?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was unforeseeable. There would be a lull of a few hours, then it would start again, and then it would stop. There was no pattern. There was no reason we could discern why it started or stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just given us one of your own personal experiences of sniper shot. Can you tell us, please, where that was that you and your daughter had to take the risky crossing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was at the crossing between the hygienic institute and Skenderija, in the very centre of town, which lies open towards Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you were able to tell where the shot was coming from or where the shooting was coming from, from that place?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was obvious, because there were a few big trees there and you could see the bullet flying through the leaves and hitting the asphalt or person, if it hit someone. And it was obviously coming from the hill, from the mountain, a few hundred metres behind Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have mentioned, I believe, that there were obviously other areas, other places where this happened. What kind of features indicated -- made for the places where the sniping took place? In other words, is there some particular feature about an area that made it more vulnerable to it being sniped upon?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: The centre of town, where the streets are wider and where the streets run at a right angle to the long axis of the town, this is where there was most sniping, and these streets were very dangerous to cross. People made detours to avoid them. And also the streets on both banks of the river Miljacka, where there were open spaces without buildings, this was also exposed to this kind of fire. The narrower streets, or the parts where the buildings are taller, these were safer, so that for the first few weeks the townspeople learned which streets and crossings were dangerous and which were less dangerous, and this applied to every part of town, but I have simply described the centre, around the assembly, the Holiday Inn hotel, the barracks, where the army had moved out, but this was all exposed, because the army of Karadzic's Serbs and their snipers were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the city Presidency have any responsibility for the sort of public safety in the sense of the infrastructure and trying to arrange safety measures for the population of Sarajevo in those conditions?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: As regards public utilities, the Presidency had exclusive responsibility for this. But as regards security, protection from sniping and shelling, the Presidency had no responsibility for this, but it did look after the security of citizens by taking care that communications were established and that people could move around under these conditions that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did the Presidency, of which you were part, have any role in contacting others about protection for the citizens in respect of this sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian defence of the town of Sarajevo, according to its establishment, was under the republican staff, so that the commander came from the republican staff, but the town civil defence, its commander was a member of the city Presidency, and it obeyed the instructions of the Presidency of the town in connection with helping to maintain the infrastructure of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, did the civilian protection do anything to try and assist protecting civilians from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, the local organisations of the civilian protection set up trash containers or buses or trucks that had been burnt, where there had been fires, they put them there on their own initiative, to make movements safer. Later on, the city Presidency organised and the civilian protection carried out the setting up of large containers from railcars that were found at the railway station in Sarajevo, and these provided better protection from the sniper shots and from the infantry weapons. Of course, machinery had to be used to move these containers. It couldn't be done by hand. So that cranes from companies that had that were recruited to move these containers by night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say when those measures started to be taken in Sarajevo, to put up the barriers against sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: This started in May. I'm referring to setting up protection on people's own initiative. Later on it was organised by the Presidency of the city and the civilian protection and companies that were able to provide the service of moving and setting up these large containers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've used the expression "people's own initiative." What do you mean by that? Was that just local community action, local residents, as it were?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo was organised into 120 local communes. These were local organisations of municipal self-government. There would be several streets or several buildings, and the inhabitants of these constituted a local commune. They would have a small administrative centre and one employee, a secretary, and the people there got together and they would put several trash containers at the end of a street to make it less exposed to sniping. So this was self-organisation without any sort of command or special organisation. So on a local level, the population tried to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later you say that the, as it were, the authorities became involved. And can you tell us what sort of criteria were applied in choosing where to put up the barricades in order? There must have been many demands, but how did you select which places to put up the barricades?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: When the city Presidency started functioning in early June, and until then the mayor's office which functioned the whole time, had been receiving reports as to where people had been wounded or killed by sniping and who these people were. So that along with general knowledge of which places were risky, there was also precise information, and if several people had been killed or wounded at a certain crossroads, this crossroads was given priority to set up this sort of passive anti-sniping protection. It took a great deal of effort to set this up, to find trucks, containers, to make a certain part of town passable in relation to snipers. One of the first crossings was the one where I had my personal experience, and containers -- two containers high, a wall two containers high was set up, because a lot of people had been wounded there, and in the centre of town, where there were more people, that was given priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us any other significant locations where in the earlier stages some of the barricades were erected, other than the junction where you had your incident?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC
utterances.text: There were anti-sniper barricades in front of the Energoinvest building, where there was a wide street. Then little by little, actually, in all the streets that were exposed and that were close to these lines outside the town from which shots were fired at the town. In Novi Grad, a lot were set up on the main road leading toward Ilidza, also on the old town on Bascarsija, which is the old centre of town. There's a big square there, where there were several rows of anti-sniper barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, would this be a suitable moment to stop? Because we have to stop at 7.00. Unless you have one short question left, but otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In fact, that's why my learned friend and I were in brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have more to say on the subject, but it's a good place to break, so indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. It is the attention of the Trial Chamber that once this witness will be excused, so after examination-in-chief, of course, cross-examination, and if necessary re-examination, that we'll have a short Status Conference and see what problems still have to be solved. So I don't know whether this will be during tomorrow, already tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, but the Court stays in recess until a quarter past 2.00 p.m. tomorrow.
